passage: "Lokesh, the loudspeaker says everyone to the school on the hill. Now." "Mummy, they said the same thing four years ago and the water never came past the gate." He was stuffing his hard drive, charger and exam notes into a bag. "Five minutes." "You said five minutes ten minutes ago." "I'm not leaving my notes to rot. Where's Papa's photo album?" "Forget the album!" "You forget it. It's the only one," he snapped, sharper than he meant. Outside, someone banged the gate and shouted Mummy's name. "Baljeet-ji! The road's already under!" Mummy grabbed his arm. "Now, Lokesh." They stepped out into water at their ankles, then at their shins by the corner. Lokesh held the bag above his head. Behind them, the album lay on the table where he'd put it down to look for the charger.

qa.q: How deep was the water by the corner?
qa.a: The water was at their shins by the corner.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh snap at Mummy about the album?
qa.a: Lokesh was tense and angry under pressure 😠 and was clinging to saving things, sure the water would stop at the gate like last time.

qa.q: Where was the turning point, and what should Lokesh have done then?
qa.a: When the loudspeaker first called everyone to the school. Leaving at once with only essentials would have spared them wading through rising water.

qa.q: What is it like for Baljeet while Lokesh keeps packing?
qa.a: Baljeet is frightened and frustrated, hearing the loudspeaker and watching the minutes slip away while Lokesh keeps asking for five more.

grounding: A young man under a real flood warning keeps packing because the water stopped at the gate before, and the family leaves late.

passage: My name is Ramesh, and last summer I learned how slow I get when I'm scared. The forest guard came up our path at dusk: the fire on the ridge had jumped the road, and every house above the temple had to go down to the school. I remember nodding as if it were an exam timetable. Fires came every summer; they always turned before reaching us. So I started packing properly, folding clothes, hunting for my certificates, wrapping Ma's brass lamp in newspaper. My sister Yamini stood at the door with the car keys, saying "Bhaiya, please," and I kept saying "one minute." Only when ash began falling on the courtyard like grey snow did my hands start to shake. We drove down with half-zipped bags. The fire did turn that night. But I know now it turned without asking me.

qa.q: What did Ramesh wrap in newspaper?
qa.a: Ma's brass lamp.

qa.q: Why was Ramesh packing slowly and carefully after the forest guard's warning?
qa.a: Ramesh was scared, as the story's first line admits, yet felt falsely sure the fire would turn like every summer, so the packing stayed slow even though the fire had jumped the road.

qa.q: What should Ramesh have done when the forest guard came, and why?
qa.a: Left at once with the essentials, because the falling ash later showed how fast things were changing; the fire's lucky turn did not make the delay safe.

qa.q: What was it like for Yamini standing at the door with the car keys?
qa.a: Yamini was scared and pleading, stuck waiting while Ramesh kept saying "one minute" and the danger grew.

grounding: A young man delays leaving during a forest fire warning, packing carefully because past fires always turned away.

passage: Camp note, Day 2. Bidisha, volunteer coordinator. Lakshmi, 19, reached the relief camp last night with her parents and grandmother, all soaked to the waist. She told me they heard the evacuation warning at five, but "everyone thought it would go down like always." Her father went back for the pump motor; Lakshmi packed her college books, then unpacked them to find her ID card. They left after dark, when water was already in the lane. She kept saying, "We had time, we had so much time," twisting her dupatta. She seemed angry, maybe at herself, maybe at her father. What I did: I sat with her, gave her dry clothes and tea, and did not lecture. This morning I asked if she would help me list what families should grab first next time. She has written half the list already.

qa.q: When did Lakshmi's family hear the evacuation warning?
qa.a: At five.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi repeating "We had time, we had so much time" suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She seems angry and full of regret, perhaps at herself or her father, realising they spent their time packing because they believed the water would go down like always.

qa.q: How did Bidisha help turn Lakshmi's regret into something useful?
qa.a: By listening without a lecture and then asking Lakshmi to help list what families should grab first, which turns a painful night into a plan for next time.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi's grandmother have experienced the late departure?
qa.a: Leaving after dark through water already in the lane would have been frightening and hard for an older person, which shows why an early start matters for the whole family.

grounding: A camp volunteer records how a young woman's family, sure the flood would pass, kept packing and left only after dark.

passage:
Night, government school hall

Diary, I'm writing this on a bench by torchlight. At four the panchayat man came up the path and said the slope behind our row of houses had cracked and we must go down to the school. Now. Amma said, "Let me finish the rice first." Appa went to tie the goats properly. I folded my college clothes, then unfolded them all to find my ID. Kavitha kept saying, "It always rains like this in July, na?" and I agreed. We've lived there nineteen years. Nothing ever slid.
We left at half past five, an hour and a half after he came. On the way down, mud was already running across the path like a brown stream. Kavitha held my hand so tight.
At seven, someone said the path we used is gone.
I keep thinking about that hour and a half.
Shalini

qa.q: What did Amma want to finish before leaving?
qa.a: She wanted to finish the rice first.

qa.q: Why did Shalini agree when Kavitha said it always rains like this in July?
qa.a: After nineteen years without a slide, the usual pattern felt safer than the warning, so Shalini believed it would pass.

qa.q: What could the family do differently the next time a warning comes?
qa.a: Keep documents and essentials packed in one bag ahead of time and leave as soon as the official warning comes, instead of finishing chores.

qa.q: What might Kavitha have felt holding Shalini's hand on the muddy path?
qa.a: Kavitha was probably frightened, realising only then how fast things were changing.

grounding: A family under a landslide warning delays leaving to finish chores and pack, sure it will pass.

passage:
Payal: the collector's order says your mandal leaves by 4. it's 3:10
Vandana: I know. papa is wrapping the tv in plastic
Vandana: mummy is making rotis for the road
Payal: vandana just go
Vandana: it always turns north at the last minute. every year
Vandana: I'm packing my certificates first, can't lose those
Payal: take the folder and go. the rest can wait
Vandana: 10 min
Payal: you said 10 min at 2:50
Vandana: the wind just ripped off the neighbour's tin roof
Payal: VANDANA
Vandana: ok we're going. papa is still arguing about taking the scooter
Payal: leave the scooter. text me from the school
Vandana: ok
Vandana: on the road. it's so much worse than it looked from inside
Payal: keep going. I'm here

qa.q: What was Papa wrapping in plastic?
qa.a: He was wrapping the TV in plastic.

qa.q: Why did Vandana keep asking for ten more minutes?
qa.a: Vandana felt confident the storm would turn north as usual, so leaving felt less urgent than saving the certificates and household things.

qa.q: What turning point finally got the family moving, and what could have moved them sooner?
qa.a: The neighbour's roof ripping off made the danger real; treating the collector's 4 o'clock order as the deadline would have moved them earlier.

qa.q: What was the chat like for Payal, watching the clock from far away?
qa.a: Payal was anxious and helpless, pushing again and again because only the messages could reach Vandana.

grounding: A family under a cyclone order delays leaving to pack and protect belongings, sure it will pass.
